questions.topicName: Blood Pressure Control: Foundations and Frameworks
questions.stem: The illustration contrasts two segments of an arteriole: the one on the left has a markedly narrowed lumen while the one on the right has a widened lumen. What is the expected effect of the change shown on the LEFT segment on systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased systemic vascular resistance and increased blood pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased systemic vascular resistance and decreased blood pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased systemic vascular resistance and increased blood pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased systemic vascular resistance and decreased blood pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: No change in systemic vascular resistance or blood pressure

explanation.summary: Narrowing of the vessel lumen (vasoconstriction) raises the resistance to blood flow through the systemic vessels, increasing systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Because blood pressure is the product of cardiac output and SVR, a rise in SVR increases blood pressure. The dilated segment on the right does the opposite, lowering SVR and blood pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Narrowing of the vessel lumen (vasoconstriction) raises the resistance to blood flow through the systemic vessels, increasing systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Because blood pressure is the product of cardiac output and SVR, a rise in SVR increases blood pressure. The dilated segment on the right does the opposite, lowering SVR and blood pressure.

questions.topicName: Blood Pressure Control: Foundations and Frameworks
questions.stem: This schematic shows a single hormone at the top branching into vasoconstriction, enhanced renal sodium/hydrogen exchange, aldosterone secretion, and release of a posterior-pituitary hormone that promotes water reabsorption. This coordinated, blood-pressure-raising response is characteristic of activation of which regulatory system?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The baroreceptor reflex arc

choices.label: B
choices.text: The kallikrein-kinin system

choices.label: C
choices.text: The natriuretic peptide system

choices.label: D
choices.text: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

choices.label: E
choices.text: The sympathetic nervous system acting alone

explanation.summary: The hormone shown branching to vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion, ADH release, and renal sodium/water reabsorption is angiotensin II, the central effector of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Its combined actions raise both systemic vascular resistance and blood volume, thereby increasing blood pressure. The natriuretic peptides and baroreceptor reflex oppose or acutely buffer pressure rather than producing this coordinated pressor response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hormone shown branching to vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion, ADH release, and renal sodium/water reabsorption is angiotensin II, the central effector of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Its combined actions raise both systemic vascular resistance and blood volume, thereby increasing blood pressure. The natriuretic peptides and baroreceptor reflex oppose or acutely buffer pressure rather than producing this coordinated pressor response.

questions.stem: This recording shows the phasic aortic pressure wave (top trace) and aortic arch baroreceptor firing (green vertical lines) across a range of mean arterial pressures. What relationship between arterial pressure and baroreceptor activity does the figure demonstrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Baroreceptor firing is constant and independent of arterial pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Baroreceptor firing frequency decreases as mean arterial pressure rises

choices.label: C
choices.text: Baroreceptor firing frequency increases as mean arterial pressure rises

choices.label: D
choices.text: Baroreceptor firing occurs only during diastole regardless of pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Baroreceptors fire only once mean arterial pressure exceeds 200 mm Hg

explanation.summary: As mean arterial pressure increases from low to high (top to bottom rows), the green firing markers become progressively denser, showing that greater arterial stretch drives a higher baroreceptor firing rate on a beat-to-beat basis. This graded, pressure-dependent firing is what allows the reflex to sense both increases and decreases in blood pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: As mean arterial pressure increases from low to high (top to bottom rows), the green firing markers become progressively denser, showing that greater arterial stretch drives a higher baroreceptor firing rate on a beat-to-beat basis. This graded, pressure-dependent firing is what allows the reflex to sense both increases and decreases in blood pressure.

questions.stem: This flowchart traces the baroreceptor reflex response to a fall in blood pressure, from reduced stretch on the carotid sinus through to the final cardiovascular output. By what mechanism does the reduced firing of the carotid sinus nerve shown here lead to increased sympathetic activity to the heart and vessels?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased afferent firing directly stimulates sympathetic ganglia in the periphery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased afferent firing triggers release of acetylcholine onto the SA node

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased afferent firing raises circulating angiotensin II, which activates sympathetic nerves

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased afferent firing removes inhibitory input to the medulla

choices.label: E
choices.text: Decreased afferent firing increases parasympathetic tone to the heart and vessels

explanation.summary: When blood pressure falls, arterial stretch and carotid sinus nerve firing decrease. Because this afferent signal normally restrains the medullary sympathetic centers, its reduction disinhibits sympathetic outflow while lowering parasympathetic activity, raising heart rate, contractility, and vascular resistance to restore blood pressure toward normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: When blood pressure falls, arterial stretch and carotid sinus nerve firing decrease. Because this afferent signal normally restrains the medullary sympathetic centers, its reduction disinhibits sympathetic outflow while lowering parasympathetic activity, raising heart rate, contractility, and vascular resistance to restore blood pressure toward normal.

questions.stem: This schematic shows the synthesis of a vasodilating peptide from its precursor during inflammation. From which cells is this peptide primarily released?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mast cells and basophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Renal collecting-duct principal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vascular endothelial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Posterior pituitary neurons

choices.label: E
choices.text: Atrial cardiomyocytes

explanation.summary: The diagram depicts bradykinin synthesis: kallikrein cleaves kininogen to yield bradykinin, causing vasodilatation. Like histamine, bradykinin is released mainly by mast cells and basophils during inflammation. Endothelial cells release NO and endothelin, atrial cardiomyocytes release ANP, and the posterior pituitary releases ADH.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagram depicts bradykinin synthesis: kallikrein cleaves kininogen to yield bradykinin, causing vasodilatation. Like histamine, bradykinin is released mainly by mast cells and basophils during inflammation. Endothelial cells release NO and endothelin, atrial cardiomyocytes release ANP, and the posterior pituitary releases ADH.

questions.stem: This cross-sectional illustration of an arterial wall labels several concentric layers. Which structural feature primarily allows a large elastic artery to expand during systole and recoil during diastole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The adventitial connective tissue sheath alone

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single layer of endothelial cells lining the lumen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rigid collagen fibers that resist any deformation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Valves within the vessel wall directing flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Elastic membranes and elastin fibers within the wall

explanation.summary: The internal and external elastic membranes and abundant elastin allow large arteries to stretch as blood is ejected in systole and recoil in diastole, sustaining pressure between beats; collagen provides tensile strength and smooth muscle adjusts tone, but elastic tissue drives the reversible expansion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The internal and external elastic membranes and abundant elastin allow large arteries to stretch as blood is ejected in systole and recoil in diastole, sustaining pressure between beats; collagen provides tensile strength and smooth muscle adjusts tone, but elastic tissue drives the reversible expansion.

questions.stem: This histologic section places a femoral artery beside a femoral vein at the same magnification. What accounts for the artery having a much thicker, rounder wall than the adjacent vein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Higher pressure and wall tension require more elastin and collagen

choices.label: B
choices.text: The artery carries a larger blood volume than the vein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Arterial blood viscosity erodes the venous wall over time

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vein is filled with valves that thin its wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: The artery has a smaller radius, demanding a thicker wall

explanation.summary: Arteries are exposed to high pressures and large radii, so by the law of Laplace they experience high wall tension and require thick walls rich in elastin and collagen; veins operate at low pressure and thus have thin, less muscular walls, giving the collapsed, thin-walled appearance seen here.
explanation.whyCorrect: Arteries are exposed to high pressures and large radii, so by the law of Laplace they experience high wall tension and require thick walls rich in elastin and collagen; veins operate at low pressure and thus have thin, less muscular walls, giving the collapsed, thin-walled appearance seen here.

questions.stem: A clinician places the bell of a stethoscope over the antecubital fossa while inflating and slowly deflating an inflatable cuff around the upper arm, as shown. What auditory phenomenon is being used to determine the systolic and diastolic pressures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Valvular closure clicks transmitted from the aortic valve

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pericardial friction rub amplified by cuff compression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Onset and disappearance of Korotkoff sounds

choices.label: D
choices.text: Venous hum produced by collapse of the brachial vein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Continuous laminar flow murmur heard throughout deflation

explanation.summary: The sphygmomanometer cuff is inflated above systolic pressure to occlude the brachial artery; as it deflates, turbulent flow through the partially compressed artery produces Korotkoff sounds. The first sound marks systolic pressure and their disappearance marks diastolic pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sphygmomanometer cuff is inflated above systolic pressure to occlude the brachial artery; as it deflates, turbulent flow through the partially compressed artery produces Korotkoff sounds. The first sound marks systolic pressure and their disappearance marks diastolic pressure.

questions.stem: The arterial pressure waveform diagram marks a small notch on the descending limb just after the peak. What event does this notch represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Closure of the aortic valve

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peak of atrial contraction (the a wave)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Onset of isovolumetric ventricular contraction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reflected pressure wave from the arterioles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Opening of the mitral valve during rapid filling

explanation.summary: The incisura (dicrotic notch) on the arterial waveform reflects aortic valve closure at the end of systole, briefly interrupting the pressure decline and separating systolic from diastolic phases; the following dicrotic wave results from brief backward flow against the closed valve.
explanation.whyCorrect: The incisura (dicrotic notch) on the arterial waveform reflects aortic valve closure at the end of systole, briefly interrupting the pressure decline and separating systolic from diastolic phases; the following dicrotic wave results from brief backward flow against the closed valve.

questions.stem: This figure plots arterial (red) and venous blood pressures along the body in the recumbent versus upright positions. Why do the arterial and venous pressures in the lower extremities rise markedly in the upright panel compared with the recumbent panel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The heart increases stroke volume to perfuse the legs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gravity adds a hydrostatic column of pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Arterial compliance falls to zero when standing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Venous valves generate active pressure in the standing position

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sympathetic vasoconstriction directly raises capillary pressure

explanation.summary: In the upright position gravity pulls blood toward the feet, adding a hydrostatic pressure column so both arterial and venous pressures in the dependent legs increase; the driving gradient between arteries and veins nonetheless stays roughly constant at 85-95 mmHg.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the upright position gravity pulls blood toward the feet, adding a hydrostatic pressure column so both arterial and venous pressures in the dependent legs increase; the driving gradient between arteries and veins nonetheless stays roughly constant at 85-95 mmHg.

questions.stem: Three vessels are each injected with the same bolus while a syringe adds fluid. In panel A the pressure change is zero for a large volume, in panel B the volume change is large for no pressure change, and in panel C both rise. Which property differs across these three panels?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elastance measured as change in pressure per change in volume equalling infinity in panel B

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrostatic pressure imposed by gravity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wall tension described by the law of Laplace

choices.label: D
choices.text: Systemic vascular resistance to steady flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vascular compliance (change in volume per change in pressure)

explanation.summary: Compliance is volume change divided by pressure change. Panel A shows zero compliance (stiff, noncompliant), panel B shows infinite compliance (large volume change, no pressure change), and panel C shows finite compliance typical of most real vessels where both pressure and volume increase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Compliance is volume change divided by pressure change. Panel A shows zero compliance (stiff, noncompliant), panel B shows infinite compliance (large volume change, no pressure change), and panel C shows finite compliance typical of most real vessels where both pressure and volume increase.

questions.stem: These pressure-volume curves compare the aorta and the vena cava. The vena cava curve is steep and flat at low pressures but flattens into a plateau at high pressures. What explains the plateau at unphysiologically high venous pressures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The vein ruptures, releasing pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elastic fibers become fully stretched

choices.label: C
choices.text: Smooth muscle actively contracts to resist further filling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gravity redistributes blood away from the vein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aortic recoil transmits pressure back to the vena cava

explanation.summary: At low pressures the floppy vena cava is highly compliant and rounds out as it fills; once fully distended its elastic fibers are maximally stretched, so additional volume produces large pressure rises and compliance falls, giving the plateau. The aorta, with thicker muscular walls, is far less compliant throughout.
explanation.whyCorrect: At low pressures the floppy vena cava is highly compliant and rounds out as it fills; once fully distended its elastic fibers are maximally stretched, so additional volume produces large pressure rises and compliance falls, giving the plateau. The aorta, with thicker muscular walls, is far less compliant throughout.

questions.stem: The paired diagram contrasts the aorta during systole versus diastole. During diastole the aortic valve is closed yet blood continues to move toward the capillaries. What mechanism drives this diastolic forward flow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active contraction of the left ventricle during diastole

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elastic recoil of the stretched aortic wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contraction of aortic smooth muscle squeezing blood forward

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skeletal muscle pump compressing the aorta

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suction generated by the closing aortic valve

explanation.summary: During systole the aorta stretches to accommodate the stroke volume; when the aortic valve closes in diastole, the elastic aorta recoils inward, maintaining the ~80 mmHg diastolic pressure and driving blood onward to the systemic circulation even though the ventricle is not ejecting.
explanation.whyCorrect: During systole the aorta stretches to accommodate the stroke volume; when the aortic valve closes in diastole, the elastic aorta recoils inward, maintaining the ~80 mmHg diastolic pressure and driving blood onward to the systemic circulation even though the ventricle is not ejecting.

questions.stem: This figure compares three capillary wall structures. Which type is found in organs such as the liver and bone marrow and is the most permeable, allowing passage of plasma proteins and cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tight-junction capillary of the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: Discontinuous (sinusoidal) capillary

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fenestrated capillary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lymphatic capillary

choices.label: E
choices.text: Continuous capillary

explanation.summary: Discontinuous (sinusoidal) capillaries have large gaps in their wall, making them highly permeable; they are found where large substances and cells must cross, such as liver, spleen, and bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Discontinuous (sinusoidal) capillaries have large gaps in their wall, making them highly permeable; they are found where large substances and cells must cross, such as liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

questions.stem: This clinical photograph shows bilateral lower-extremity swelling with a persistent indentation left after finger pressure. What does this finding indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pretibial myxedema

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pitting edema

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cellulitis with abscess formation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Non-pitting lymphedema

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chronic venous stasis hyperpigmentation

explanation.summary: A pit that persists after pressure indicates displaceable interstitial fluid (pitting edema), typically from raised capillary hydrostatic pressure or reduced oncotic pressure, as in heart failure or nephrotic syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: A pit that persists after pressure indicates displaceable interstitial fluid (pitting edema), typically from raised capillary hydrostatic pressure or reduced oncotic pressure, as in heart failure or nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: This schematic shows fluid exchange across a capillary bed, including a blind-ended vessel (bottom) draining the surrounding interstitium. What is the primary role of that blind-ended vessel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It generates the capillary hydrostatic pressure that drives filtration

choices.label: B
choices.text: It delivers freshly oxygenated blood to the tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: It secretes plasma proteins directly into the interstitium

choices.label: D
choices.text: It returns excess interstitial fluid back to the circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the principal site of alveolar gas exchange

explanation.summary: The blind-ended lymphatic capillary collects the small excess of filtered fluid and proteins not reabsorbed at the venular end, returning them to the venous circulation and preventing interstitial fluid accumulation (edema).
explanation.whyCorrect: The blind-ended lymphatic capillary collects the small excess of filtered fluid and proteins not reabsorbed at the venular end, returning them to the venous circulation and preventing interstitial fluid accumulation (edema).

questions.stem: In this diagram of the body fluid compartments, which structure separates the two compartments that together constitute the extracellular fluid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The capillary wall, which separates plasma from interstitial fluid

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blood-brain barrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lymphatic endothelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cell membrane, which separates interstitial from intracellular fluid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The glomerular basement membrane

explanation.summary: Extracellular fluid comprises plasma (intravascular) and interstitial fluid; these are separated by the capillary wall. The cell membrane instead separates extracellular from intracellular fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extracellular fluid comprises plasma (intravascular) and interstitial fluid; these are separated by the capillary wall. The cell membrane instead separates extracellular from intracellular fluid.

questions.stem: This figure depicts how capillary hydrostatic pressure changes from the arteriolar to the venular end. Why does net filtration predominate at the arteriolar end?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capillary oncotic pressure is highest at the arteriolar end

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphatic drainage is greatest at the arteriolar end

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interstitial hydrostatic pressure is strongly positive at the arteriolar end

choices.label: D
choices.text: Capillary hydrostatic pressure there exceeds the opposing oncotic pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: The capillary wall is impermeable at the arteriolar end

explanation.summary: At the arteriolar end, high capillary hydrostatic pressure outweighs the relatively constant oncotic pressure, driving fluid out (filtration); pressure falls toward the venular end, where reabsorption dominates.
explanation.whyCorrect: At the arteriolar end, high capillary hydrostatic pressure outweighs the relatively constant oncotic pressure, driving fluid out (filtration); pressure falls toward the venular end, where reabsorption dominates.

questions.stem: In this figure, hydrostatic pressure (blue arrows) declines along the capillary length while oncotic pressure (orange) stays relatively constant. What is the net result at the venular end?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reversal of the direction of blood flow

choices.label: B
choices.text: No net movement of fluid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maximal filtration into the lymphatics

choices.label: D
choices.text: Net reabsorption of fluid into the capillary

choices.label: E
choices.text: Net filtration of fluid out of the capillary

explanation.summary: Because hydrostatic pressure falls below the roughly constant oncotic pressure toward the venular end, the balance of Starling forces favors reabsorption of fluid back into the capillary.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because hydrostatic pressure falls below the roughly constant oncotic pressure toward the venular end, the balance of Starling forces favors reabsorption of fluid back into the capillary.

questions.stem: Given the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic pressures depicted at this distal (venular) capillary, what is the direction of net fluid movement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluid moves only into the lymphatic vessels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Filtration, with fluid moving out of the capillary into the interstitium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reabsorption, with fluid moving from the interstitium into the capillary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bidirectional oscillating flow with each heartbeat

choices.label: E
choices.text: No net movement, because the forces are exactly balanced

explanation.summary: At the distal capillary the capillary oncotic pressure exceeds the reduced hydrostatic pressure, so the net Starling force draws fluid back into the vessel (reabsorption).
explanation.whyCorrect: At the distal capillary the capillary oncotic pressure exceeds the reduced hydrostatic pressure, so the net Starling force draws fluid back into the vessel (reabsorption).

questions.stem: These plots show local blood flow rising as tissue metabolic activity increases. What is the primary driver of this increase in flow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circulating epinephrine acting on beta-1 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: A rise in arterial oxygen partial pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Local accumulation of vasodilator metabolites

choices.label: D
choices.text: Baroreceptor-mediated reflex vasodilation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased sympathetic outflow to the tissue

explanation.summary: Active (functional) hyperemia results from metabolites such as CO2, H+, adenosine, and K+ accumulating during increased activity, which dilate local vessels and raise flow to match demand.
explanation.whyCorrect: Active (functional) hyperemia results from metabolites such as CO2, H+, adenosine, and K+ accumulating during increased activity, which dilate local vessels and raise flow to match demand.

questions.stem: This tracing shows a surge in blood flow above baseline immediately after a period of no flow. What produces the overshoot once the occlusion is released?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased venous return raising cardiac preload

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reflex tachycardia increasing cardiac output

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endothelin-1 released from the vessel wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sympathetic withdrawal from the occluded limb

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasodilator metabolites

explanation.summary: During occlusion, metabolites build up and cannot be washed away; on reperfusion these dilators cause blood flow to transiently exceed baseline (reactive hyperemia).
explanation.whyCorrect: During occlusion, metabolites build up and cannot be washed away; on reperfusion these dilators cause blood flow to transiently exceed baseline (reactive hyperemia).

questions.stem: In this schematic of endothelial paracrine factors acting on vascular smooth muscle, which released factor promotes contraction rather than relaxation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: L-arginine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor (EDHF)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prostacyclin (PGI2)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endothelin-1 (ET-1)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nitric oxide (NO)

explanation.summary: The endothelium releases both dilators (NO, EDHF, PGI2) and constrictors; endothelin-1 is the potent vasoconstrictor, promoting smooth muscle contraction while the others favor relaxation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The endothelium releases both dilators (NO, EDHF, PGI2) and constrictors; endothelin-1 is the potent vasoconstrictor, promoting smooth muscle contraction while the others favor relaxation.

questions.stem: This diagram traces the pathway from endothelial stimulation through to vascular smooth muscle relaxation. What second messenger directly mediates the relaxation shown?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diacylglycerol (DAG)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyclic GMP (cGMP)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inositol trisphosphate (IP3)

choices.label: D
choices.text: The calcium-calmodulin complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cyclic AMP (cAMP)

explanation.summary: Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP, which lowers intracellular calcium and activates myosin light chain phosphatase to relax vascular smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP, which lowers intracellular calcium and activates myosin light chain phosphatase to relax vascular smooth muscle.

questions.stem: These tracings compare two catecholamines' effects on arterial pressure and heart rate. Why does the agent on the left produce little net change in mean arterial pressure at physiologic doses while the agent on the right raises it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epinephrine triggers reflex bradycardia that lowers output

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epinephrine does not bind adrenergic receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Norepinephrine preferentially activates beta-2 receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epinephrine's beta-2 vasodilation offsets its pressor effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Norepinephrine has no effect on alpha-1 receptors

explanation.summary: At physiologic levels epinephrine engages beta-2 receptors causing skeletal muscle vasodilation, which counterbalances its alpha-mediated pressor action; norepinephrine acts mainly on alpha-1, so it raises MAP and triggers reflex bradycardia.
explanation.whyCorrect: At physiologic levels epinephrine engages beta-2 receptors causing skeletal muscle vasodilation, which counterbalances its alpha-mediated pressor action; norepinephrine acts mainly on alpha-1, so it raises MAP and triggers reflex bradycardia.

questions.stem: The bedside positioning maneuver depicted is used to acutely support blood pressure in a hypotensive patient. By what primary mechanism does it raise blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reduces intrathoracic pressure, enhancing coronary artery filling

choices.label: B
choices.text: It stimulates renal sodium and water retention to expand plasma volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: It directly increases myocardial contractility through baroreceptor activation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It uses gravity to shift blood from the legs, increasing venous return

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reflexively lowers systemic vascular resistance to improve perfusion

explanation.summary: Tilting the patient head-down (legs elevated) uses gravity to redistribute pooled venous blood from the lower extremities toward the central circulation, transiently increasing venous return, preload, stroke volume, and thus cardiac output and blood pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tilting the patient head-down (legs elevated) uses gravity to redistribute pooled venous blood from the lower extremities toward the central circulation, transiently increasing venous return, preload, stroke volume, and thus cardiac output and blood pressure.

questions.stem: This 12-lead ECG shows a regular rhythm with a consistent 1:1 P-to-QRS relationship and normal waveform morphology at a notably slow rate. What is the underlying rhythm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Junctional escape rhythm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sinoatrial exit block

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sinus bradycardia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Second-degree AV block

explanation.summary: A slow rate with an upright P wave preceding every QRS in a 1:1 fashion and normal PR interval indicates the impulse still originates in the SA node, defining sinus bradycardia rather than a junctional, blocked, or ectopic rhythm.
explanation.whyCorrect: A slow rate with an upright P wave preceding every QRS in a 1:1 fashion and normal PR interval indicates the impulse still originates in the SA node, defining sinus bradycardia rather than a junctional, blocked, or ectopic rhythm.

questions.stem: This ECG illustration counts the small boxes between two consecutive R waves to calculate heart rate. What calculation does this method use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Multiply the number of small boxes by 0.04 seconds

choices.label: B
choices.text: Divide 300 by the number of large boxes between R waves

choices.label: C
choices.text: Count QRS complexes in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10

choices.label: D
choices.text: Divide 60 by the R-R interval measured in large boxes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Divide 1500 by the number of small boxes between R waves

explanation.summary: The precise R-R small-box method divides 1500 (small boxes per minute at 25 mm/s) by the number of small boxes between consecutive R waves to yield beats per minute.
explanation.whyCorrect: The precise R-R small-box method divides 1500 (small boxes per minute at 25 mm/s) by the number of small boxes between consecutive R waves to yield beats per minute.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at roughly 130 bpm with a normal upright P wave preceding every QRS. What rhythm is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrial fibrillation with rapid response

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sinus tachycardia

choices.label: C
choices.text: AV nodal reentrant tachycardia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Focal atrial tachycardia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction

explanation.summary: A fast but regular rhythm with a normal P wave before each QRS and a constant PR interval indicates the SA node is simply firing faster, defining sinus tachycardia rather than a reentrant or ectopic tachyarrhythmia.
explanation.whyCorrect: A fast but regular rhythm with a normal P wave before each QRS and a constant PR interval indicates the SA node is simply firing faster, defining sinus tachycardia rather than a reentrant or ectopic tachyarrhythmia.
